scope_plain: Voters in Colorado's 1st Congressional District: all of Denver plus Glendale. Three certified write-in candidates (Kevin StClair and John Wren, both Democrats, and Stephen Replin, unaffiliated) are not printed on the ballot; to vote for one, write the name on the write-in line.
office_explainer: Denver's one seat in the U.S. House. Votes on federal laws, taxes and spending.
why_it_matters: Open seat for the first time since 1996. Rep. Diana DeGette lost the June Democratic primary to Melat Kiros. The district has not elected a Republican since 1970; about 230,000 of its 464,000 active voters are unaffiliated.
incumbent: Diana DeGette (lost primary; not on ballot)

candidates.name: Melat Kiros
candidates.background: 29. Daughter of Ethiopian immigrants, graduate student and former attorney; she says Sidley Austin fired her after she defended students' right to protest the war in Gaza. Until recently a tipped-wage barista. Identifies as a democratic socialist. Beat 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette in the June 30 primary.

own_words.text: Top priorities: "Healthcare, housing, and ending the corruption blocking both."
"I'll fight for Medicare for All to cut out the insurance middlemen." Supports Housing First policies and federal money for housing production.
"Congress needs to abolish ICE and build something humane." Says she has never taken corporate PAC money and never will.

candidates.name: Christy Peterson
candidates.background: Accountant; Colorado born and raised; describes herself as a construction manager, notary and "tax guru." Did not answer the Denver Gazette but did answer the Denver Post.

own_words.text: Top three priorities: "Safety, Economy & Education."
"I support the President, his agendas and tax breaks."
Says Denver's sanctuary policy "invites illegal migrants, taking up housing, making prices higher."

candidates.name: Critter Milton
candidates.background: Unity Party nominee. No campaign site or questionnaire answers found.

own_words.text: Did not return the Denver Post questionnaire.

candidates.name: Chad Humphrey
candidates.background: Tech manager and entrepreneur; retired Marine Corps officer and combat veteran; MBA from Pepperdine.

own_words.text: "Turn Off the Money Printer: Stop federal spending, audit the Fed, and end corporate bailouts."
Would "End warrantless government surveillance," including Flock license-plate cameras, and cut the power of regulatory agencies.
"End Ego-Driven Wars": stop acting as the world's police and reclaim war powers.

candidates.name: Shimon Blau
candidates.background: 50. Board-certified physician with 20-plus years in practice and a small business owner. Born in Denver's Sloan's Lake neighborhood to immigrant parents. Launched his campaign and petitioned onto the ballot within days of the June primary.

own_words.text: Top priorities: "affordability, healthcare reform, and economic growth."
"Our country needs a strong, secure border" but also wants to "fast-track legal status for long-term, contributing members of our communities."
Says he will "stand up to Trump" for all his constituents, takes no PAC money, and wants to restore federal funding cut from local hospitals and health programs.

scope_plain: Voters in Colorado's 6th Congressional District: Aurora, Centennial, Littleton and Englewood areas in Arapahoe County, plus a small piece of far northeast Denver. Most Denver voters are in CD-1, not CD-6.
office_explainer: One of Colorado's eight seats in the U.S. House. Votes on federal laws, taxes and spending.
why_it_matters: Rep. Jason Crow is seeking a fifth term in a district that leans Democratic. Covered here because the Denver sample ballot includes it and because Aurora and Englewood voters are in it.

candidates.name: Jason Crow
candidates.background: U.S. representative since 2019; former Army Ranger and paratrooper; lives in Aurora. Heads the End Corruption Caucus.

own_words.text: Priorities: "Lowering the costs of housing, healthcare, gas, and groceries, cleaning up corruption," and "ending forever wars in the Middle East."
Says Trump's "illegal war with Iran, reckless tariffs, and rampant corruption have raised prices."
"It's the job and duty of Congress to provide a check and balance on the Executive Branch."

candidates.name: Jason Clark
candidates.background: Entrepreneur and West Point graduate; former Army officer; lives in Aurora.

own_words.text: Top three priorities: "1. Limited government. 2. Limited government. 3. Limited government." Answered every Post question with the same two words.

candidates.name: Patty McMahon
candidates.background: Publisher; 35 years with the EEOC; lives in Littleton.

own_words.text: "Fix how government spends": rein in federal spending and the national debt.
"Restore the separation of powers" including Congress's role in war and peace; expand lifelong credentialed education through 'O.P.E.N. America.'

candidates.name: Meredith Ryan
candidates.background: Unity Party nominee.

own_words.text: Did not return the Denver Post questionnaire.

candidates.name: Samir Witta
candidates.background: Oncologist for 25 years in the district; PhD; founded nonprofits on patient costs; lives in Cherry Hills.

own_words.text: "Cap medical deductibles by law, lower premiums, mandate drug price transparency."
Wants to reform "predatory HOA practices" and stop corporate consolidation driving rents.
"Serve District 6 first, party never." Takes no corporate PAC money.

scope_plain: Voters in Congressional District 1 (Denver and nearby slivers)
office_explainer: Sets statewide K-12 rules: academic standards, graduation requirements, charter appeals, school ratings.
why_it_matters: The nine-member board oversees the Colorado Department of Education and decides charter school appeals and how struggling schools are handled. Six-year term.

candidates.name: Lisa Escárcega
candidates.background: Incumbent, first elected 2020. Over 40 years in education: school psychologist, district administrator, retired executive director of the Colorado Association of School Executives. Ed.S. and Ph.D.

own_words.text: Says that after "decades of tax cuts and the constraints of TABOR," Colorado "must find revenue that ensures adequate and equitable funding" for public schools.
Wants alternative pathways into teaching and mental health jobs to address the educator shortage, and "an inclusive public education for all."
Says the state school-rating system is "over reliant on our current measures" and should include local performance data.

office: Regent of the University of Colorado
scope_plain: Voters in Congressional District 6 only (Aurora, Centennial, Littleton, Englewood areas, and a small piece of northeast Denver). Most Denver voters will not see this race; the CD-1 regent seat is not up in 2026.
office_explainer: One of nine elected regents who govern the University of Colorado system: tuition, budgets, the president.
why_it_matters: Regents set CU tuition and pick the university president. The board's partisan balance has flipped in recent cycles. Six-year term.

candidates.name: Ilana Spiegel
candidates.background: Incumbent regent since 2021. Educational consultant; Wellesley BA, Columbia MA in education; lives in Englewood.

own_words.text: Priorities: "affordability, access and student success, and protecting CU's academic mission."
Says CU's greatest challenge is "preserving its public mission amid financial pressure and political interference."
Points to CU Promise, the tuition guarantee and CU Denver's automatic acceptance program in CD-6.

candidates.name: Veanessa Burbage
candidates.background: Republican nominee; unopposed in the June primary.

own_words.text: Did not return the Denver Post questionnaire.

candidates.name: Joe Johnson
candidates.background: Business owner from Aurora; 30-plus years in sales and corporate training.

own_words.text: "Return education as the top priority in Higher Education"; says sports "should no longer be job #1."
Calls the 'College for All' mentality "disastrous" and wants less government involvement in higher education.

sources.name: Denver Post CU Regent District 6 Q&A

scope_plain: Voters in Senate District 31 (central and southeast Denver). This is a special election for the last two years of the current term.
office_explainer: One of 35 state senators. Writes state laws and the state budget at the Capitol.
why_it_matters: Only one name is on the ballot. Sen. Chris Hansen won this seat in 2024 and resigned; a Democratic vacancy committee picked Matt Ball in January 2025. This election fills the last two years of that term. (A Critical Report primary recap named Republican Michael DiManna as a primary winner, but he is not on the SOS certified list or the Denver ballot.)

candidates.name: Matt Ball
candidates.background: State senator since January 2025, picked by a Democratic vacancy committee after Sen. Chris Hansen resigned. Army veteran (101st Airborne and 75th Ranger Regiment) and Army Reservist; Stanford law degree; former policy director for the City of Denver. Only candidate on the ballot.

own_words.text: Campaign site: "As a father, veteran, and dedicated public servant, Matt brings lived experience and a track record of results."
His campaign says he passed the most bills of any first-term legislator in the 2025 session.

scope_plain: Voters in Senate District 32 (south and southwest Denver)
office_explainer: One of 35 state senators. Writes state laws and the state budget at the Capitol.
why_it_matters: Open seat. Senate Majority Leader Robert Rodriguez is term-limited.

candidates.name: Emily Sirota
candidates.background: State representative for House District 9 since 2019. Won the June Democratic primary.

own_words.text: Making the tax code fairer for working people
We can prevent huge data centers from passing on electricity costs to residential consumers.
We can increase access to affordable child care and education if we pass a graduated income tax

candidates.background: Republican nominee.

why_it_matters: Open seat. Sen. Julie Gonzales, first elected in 2018, is term-limited; she ran for U.S. Senate and lost the June Democratic primary to John Hickenlooper. Four-year term.

candidates.name: Chela Garcia Irlando
candidates.background: Nonprofit director. Won the June Democratic primary with 69% over Andrés Carrera. Listed as Graciela "Chela" Garcia Irlando by the state party. Did not participate in the Denver Gazette voter guide.

own_words.text: Did not answer the Denver Gazette questionnaire. No campaign site located as of Oct 16.

candidates.name: Jennifer Qualteri
candidates.background: Republican nominee. Says she does not take monetary donations.

own_words.text: "A structural deficit is a spending problem dressed up as a revenue shortage." Would protect policing, roads and classroom instruction and "freeze and audit everything else."
On housing: "legalize more homes on more parcels," cut permit timelines, no statewide rent control.
"Colorado should stop pretending mandates are free." Wants to keep gas and nuclear on the table and repeal rules that force early plant shutdowns.

candidates.name: Jacob Luria
candidates.background: Libertarian nominee.

own_words.text: Affordable Housing & Faster Approvals, Support CO-Owned Businesses & Workers and Improving Infrastructure.
Reduce permitting time and cost at a state level and reform Jared Polis’ ADU bill to make it less restrictive.
We need to rein in government spending and make the spending more transparent to the public.

office_explainer: One of 65 state representatives. Writes state laws and the state budget at the Capitol.
why_it_matters: Incumbent seeks a third term.

candidates.name: Javier Mabrey
candidates.background: Incumbent since 2023. Eviction defense attorney. Describes himself as a progressive Democrat.

own_words.text: Colorado is the only state that makes workers win two elections to form a strong union.
We should ban landlords from using algorithms to fix the price of rents
Pass a bill that creates a civil cause of action when your constitutional rights are violated by federal agents.

candidates.name: Joseph Montoya
candidates.background: Financial professional; won the June Republican primary.

own_words.text: Remove the 10 year requirement for senior citizens to receive the tax credit.
I have a plan to reform family court, using the same model as drug court.
I would like to put rent control in place to address homelessness.

office_explainer: One of 65 state representatives. Writes state laws and the state budget at the Capitol.
why_it_matters: Open seat.

candidates.name: Scott Baldermann
candidates.background: Former Denver Board of Education member (2019 to 2023) and business owner.

own_words.text: "I've built businesses and created jobs here in Colorado, and advocated for our community for more than a decade."
Priorities listed: accountable public investment, accessible health care and affordable housing, affordable capital for small businesses, expanded transit and clean energy.

candidates.name: Carey Marin
candidates.background: Business owner; won the June Republican primary.

own_words.text: We must increase housing supply by reducing regulatory barriers, permitting delays and other government-imposed costs
Priorities listed: cost of living, reducing government spending, and homelessness, plus protecting TABOR and voters' right to approve tax increases.

own_words.text: Priorities: "Reproductive Rights," "Labor Rights" and "Equity." Slogan: "Action Over Talk."

candidates.name: Rebecca Winegar
candidates.background: Won the June Republican primary. Critical Report describes her as an anti-abortion activist; her site says she holds the NRA-PVF's AQ rating.

own_words.text: "A common-sense Republican fighting for safer streets, lower taxes, better schools."
Cites a $1.2 billion state budget shortfall and a 40% property tax increase since 2023 as reasons to end "one-party rule at the State Capitol."

candidates.background: Won the June Republican primary (Critical Report spells it Erwin; the SOS list says Ervin).

own_words.text: No platform collected yet.

candidates.name: Cecelia Espenoza
candidates.background: Incumbent. Former immigration appellate judge, attorney and University of Denver law professor. Has lived in the district 34 years.

own_words.text: Priorities on her site: "Justice that works for people," "Safer communities. Smarter solutions," and "Keeping Colorado affordable for families and businesses."

candidates.name: Bill Hare
candidates.background: Forward Party nominee.

candidates.background: Fifth-generation Coloradan from North Denver; political director who spent nearly a decade at NARAL Pro-Choice Colorado (now Cobalt). Won the June primary with 77%.

own_words.text: "I come from a family of activists who fought for Chicano rights in Denver," and says that fighting spirit shapes her.
Background in reproductive-rights advocacy, transportation access and environmental justice organizing.

candidates.name: Johnnie W. Johnson
candidates.background: Republican nominee in 2022 and 2024 as well.

candidates.name: Iris Halpern
candidates.background: Civil rights and workers' rights attorney, formerly with the EEOC. Beat incumbent Rep. Sean Camacho in the June primary, 55% to 45%.

own_words.text: "It's time for a fighter." Calls herself "a career-long civil and workers' rights attorney."
Priorities: civil rights and bodily autonomy, housing affordability, "make big polluters pay," affordable health care, school funding, gun control.

candidates.name: Kathleen Angel
candidates.background: Campus coordinator; won the June Republican primary.

office_explainer: One of 65 state representatives. Writes state laws and the state budget at the Capitol.
why_it_matters: No Republican on the ballot.

candidates.name: Jennifer Bacon
candidates.background: Incumbent since 2021; former Denver school board member, teacher, community organizer and attorney.

own_words.text: Says she sought to "educate in the classroom, build power with families as a community organizer and attorney, and partner with neighbors" on legislation.

candidates.name: Jeff Wilson
candidates.background: Libertarian nominee. No Republican qualified.

own_words.text: Eliminating homelessness while reducing the budget by vastly increasing the use of strategically placed pallet shelter communities
Abolish single-family and other non-safety-related zoning laws.
Wants proportional representation for the state legislature and ranked choice voting.

candidates.name: Lindsay Gilchrist
candidates.background: Incumbent since 2025. Born and raised in Denver; policy professional. Says she passed 26 bills in her first term and chairs the House Health and Human Services Committee.

own_words.text: "Government should be a place where we come together to solve real problems."

candidates.name: Jesse Lashawn Parris
candidates.background: Unity Party nominee; frequent Denver City Council public commenter.

own_words.text: Lists his priorities as stopping displacement, accountability in public safety, and the interests of Black Denverites.
Cap utility rate increases from monopolies
Tax speculative land banking and luxury developments to fund permanent affordable housing!

scope_plain: Voters in RTD Director District B (north and northeast Denver, including Montbello, Green Valley Ranch and DIA, plus Aurora north of Colfax in Adams County). Check your ballot; Denver is split among RTD districts A, B, C, D and E, and only B and C have elections this year.
office_explainer: One of 15 directors who run RTD: bus and rail routes, fares, budget. Nonpartisan.
why_it_matters: RTD is proposing its 2027 budget and deciding service levels and fares. Four-year term, unpaid.

candidates.name: John Glenn
candidates.background: Architect (M.Arch and BFA); transit commuter for 35 years. Says he has spent his career connecting housing, transit and affordability. Raised about $20,000 through mid-September.

own_words.text: "At this moment RTD doesn't need another politician, it needs a builder."
Priorities: make transit "reliable, frequent, clean, and safe"; use RTD land for housing at stations … new leadership with "less politics, more accountability."
"RTD needs to build ridership, not simply cut service." Says a 2028 ballot measure "should remain on the table" as a bridge.

candidates.name: Bianka Emerson
candidates.background: Political strategist with 20-plus years in public policy, coalition building, affordable housing and environmental justice; president of Colorado Black Women for Political Action; Southern University graduate and trained lawyer. Raised about $2,900 through mid-September.

own_words.text: Priorities: "Reliable and Equitable Service," "Safe, Accessible Transit & Connected Communities," and "Accountability & Community Voice."
"I support the ballot measure because RTD needs sustainable revenue." Would oppose fare increases "that price out riders."
Hears most about late buses, limited District B routes, inconsistent light rail and safety; says "operators should not be expected to serve as social workers."

office_explainer: One of 15 directors who run RTD: bus and rail routes, fares, budget. Nonpartisan.
why_it_matters: Only one candidate qualified, so the race is effectively decided. Four-year term, unpaid.

candidates.name: Joe Meyer
candidates.background: Aerospace engineer (BS/MS mechanical engineering, Colorado School of Mines); transit rider and member of RTD's Citizens Advisory Committee. Only candidate on the ballot. Endorsed by the Democratic Party of Denver.

own_words.text: Priorities: "reliability combined with convenience" along major corridors, and "speed up decision making by investing more in pilot projects."
"I don't believe RTD's budget shortfall can be fixed with efficiency gains or cost cuts alone." Supports a voter-referred revenue measure
Would push dedicated lanes, signal priority and in-lane boarding, and refocus security on the code of conduct rather than fare enforcement.

office: Denver City Council, At-Large Seat B (vacancy election)
office_explainer: One of two citywide council seats. Council passes Denver's laws, budget and contracts.
why_it_matters: Special election to fill the seat Sarah Parady left in August. The winner serves until the regular city election in spring 2027 picks someone for a new term starting in July 2027. Whoever gets the most votes wins; there is no runoff. Two front-runners have similar names: Monica Martinez (9th name on the ballot), who runs the Fax Partnership on East Colfax, and Melissa Adriana Mejía (7th), a housing policy strategist. Both say voters mix them up, so check the full name before you mark.

candidates.name: Alfredo Reyes
candidates.background: 36. Nonprofit executive; west-side native and son of immigrants.

own_words.text: Top issue: "Affordability." Wants Denver to "build across the life span: three- and four-bedroom homes alongside childcare, amenities, and grocery stores."
On data centers: "We cannot drink data." Wants corporations to innovate on water and energy before asking Denver for anything.
"I will never vote on a contract I have not read." Would cut corporate subsidies and premium outside contracts first; would not privatize basic services.

candidates.name: Whitney Traylor
candidates.background: 55. Denver attorney (Traylor Law Group).

own_words.text: Top issue: Denver "keeps paying for its own mistakes," citing more than $30 million in police-related settlements since 2020. Proposes a public settlement tracker and root-cause reviews.
Supports the data center moratorium; says Denver already has about 50 data centers and more would strain water and raise grid costs.
Would cut outside legal spending and unproven consultant contracts; "I would not privatize core services."

candidates.name: Jeff Walker
candidates.background: 61. Former elected RTD board member.

own_words.text: "The number one issue is traffic safety." Would press to lower speed limits on all Denver streets.
Would exclude data centers over 50,000 square feet within a quarter mile of residential zones.
Says Denver spends too much on police patrol and should make the STAR crisis-response program a 24-hour service.

candidates.name: Julissa Soto
candidates.background: Founder of Julissa Soto Latino Health Equity Consulting and Casa Inmigrante. Did not respond to the Denver Gazette or Denver Post questionnaires.

own_words.text: Did not respond to the Denver Gazette questionnaire.

candidates.name: Gabriel Konkle
candidates.background: 37. Software architect.

own_words.text: Would introduce an ordinance requiring a judicial warrant for any technology-assisted surveillance (license plate readers, police drones).
"We must ban data centers and protect our neighborhoods."
Calls the roughly $25 million a year spent on 3,000 acres of manicured grass "a waste"; wants more money for STAR and less for incarceration.

candidates.name: Cynthia Diaz
candidates.background: 46. Owns Tonantzin Casa de Café on Santa Fe Drive.

own_words.text: "Small businesses are closing across Denver, and the city is making it worse." Wants construction-mitigation money built into project budgets.
No new data centers "until Denver writes rules that protect our most vulnerable residents, our water, and our environment." No tax breaks.
"Privatization is not the answer. Trash is essential." Says the sales-tax-heavy budget is a structural weakness, so grow the small-business base.

candidates.name: Melissa Adriana Mejía
candidates.background: 41. Housing policy strategist; director of state and local policy at the Community Economic Defense Project; former aide in Council District 3. Raised on Denver's north and west sides; member of Denver DSA.

own_words.text: Top issue: affordability. "Growth is inevitable, but displacement doesn't have to be." Supports tenant protections and public and nonprofit housing development.
"Denver should not allow hyperscale data centers." Supports the current moratorium.
"Denver should spend less subsidizing wealthy corporations and more on the services that make life affordable."

candidates.name: Jake Browne
candidates.background: 43. Marketing director. Takes part in the Fair Elections Fund ($415 cap per donor, no corporate or PAC money) and publishes his receipts.

own_words.text: Top issue: people leaving Denver. Would open the property tax relief program to working renters, since "Renters pay property tax, too. It's in the rent."
On data centers: "If they want to be in Denver, they pay us instead of the other way around."
"Every contract should prove it worked before it renews." Would grow STAR; would not privatize trash; "I won't tax the poor to help the poor."

candidates.name: Monica Martinez
candidates.background: 52. Executive director of the Fax Partnership, an East Colfax nonprofit for residents and businesses, since 2015. Lifelong Democrat who says she is "more circumspect" about some DSA policies.

own_words.text: "If you live in Denver, you should be able to afford to stay in Denver." Wants housing near transit and better neighborhood connections.
Supports "responsible development" of data centers with strong environmental and labor standards and recycled-water design.
Says government growth from 2010 to 2020 "must now be reined in" and regulations cut to reduce the "time tax" on local businesses.

candidates.name: Raymon Anthony Doane
candidates.background: 36. Tax professional.

own_words.text: Would support district-level shelters and "case-by-case plans pairing enforcement with voluntary treatment/housing services."
Says additional data centers "should face scrutiny given high energy/water use."
Wants "greater efficiency to cut waste" and to evaluate where services can be delivered more cost-effectively.

candidates.background: 43. Incumbent since 2023 (BS, JD, MA). Won the June primary with 65%.

"I oppose tax incentives for data centers." Skeptical hyperscale facilities can be made sustainable.
